claim: The computational model uses the upper extremity biomechanical model introduced by Saul et al., 2015.
source: Our computational model uses the upper extremity biomechanical model introduced by Saul et al., 2015 and available at https://simtk.org/projects/upexdyn.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by a citation to Saul et al., 2015.

claim: The biomechanical model consists of 47 Hill-type muscle-tendon actuators.
source: The model consists of 47 Hill-type muscle-tendon actuators (Zajac, 1989) with parameters and paths derived from experimental and anatomical studies.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zajac, 1989 and reference to experimental and anatomical studies.

claim: The skeletal model has five degrees-of-freedom representing the shoulder, elbow, and forearm.
source: The skeletal model has five degrees-of-freedom representing the shoulder (elevation plane, elevation angle, and shoulder rotation), the elbow (flexion/extension), and the forearm (pronation/supination).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text describing the model structure.

claim: The simulation was performed with OpenSim and the Simbody physics engine.
source: The simulation was performed with OpenSim (Delp and Anderson, 2007) and the Simbody physics engine (Sherman et al., 2011) with a semi-explicit Euler integrator (accuracy 1e−2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Delp and Anderson, 2007 and Sherman et al., 2011.

claim: The computational model reproduces hand paths similar to those reported in Beer et al., 2000 during a center-out fast reaching task.
source: In Figure 1A and B, we compare the hand positions in a center-out fast reaching task from our model and the data reported in Beer et al., 2000.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with experimental data from Beer et al., 2000 and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The simulations reproduce the observation that arm reach trajectories are gently curved, particularly near the targets.
source: Note that our simulations reproduce the observation that arm reach trajectories (in humans and non-human primates) are gently curved, particularly near the targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with known observations in humans and non-human primates.

claim: The maximum unnormalized speed in the simulation is 1.10 m/s, which falls in the range of maximal speeds reported in Soechting, 1984.
source: The maximum unnormalized speed in Figure 1D is 1.10 m/s, which falls in the range of maximal speeds reported in Soechting, 1984 (i.e., from 0.65 m/s to 1.35 m/s).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with experimental data from Soechting, 1984.

claim: A smaller target causes the movement to have an earlier peak velocity and a velocity that decays more rapidly.
source: Soechting reported that a smaller target causes the movement to have an earlier peak velocity and a velocity that decays more rapidly. We reproduce both of these features in our simulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Soechting and reproduction in simulations.

claim: The velocity profile is symmetric for intermediate speeds and becomes asymmetric with changes in speed.
source: Several studies have shown that the velocity profile is symmetric for intermediate speeds and becomes asymmetric with changes in speed (e.g., Nagasaki, 1989; Ostry et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nagasaki, 1989 and Ostry et al., 1987.

claim: The ratio of the time to the peak velocity to the entire movement time tends to be smaller with slower movements.
source: The ratio of the time to the peak velocity to the entire movement time tends to be smaller with slower movements.
evidence: The claim is stated as an established observation in the field.

claim: The computational model reproduces the speed-dependent asymmetry in the velocity profile.
source: Our model reproduces the speed-dependent asymmetry in the velocity profile.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model's output data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The relative peak velocities are 0.66, 0.51, and 0.4 for the fast, medium, and slow movements, respectively.
source: The relative peak velocities in Figure 2C are 0.66, 0.51, and 0.4 for the fast, medium, and slow movements, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The velocity profiles of slower movements tend to exhibit multiple local minima.
source: It has also been reported that the velocity profiles of slower movements tend to exhibit multiple local minima (e.g., Soechting, 1984; van der Wel et al., 2009); we replicate these findings in our simulations (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for the velocity profile asymmetry for MDs of 0.15 s, 0.25 s, and 0.45 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Soechting, 1984 and van der Wel et al., 2009, and replicated in simulations.

claim: A torque-driven model does not reproduce the reported asymmetries in the velocity profiles.
source: In Figure 2—figure supplement 2, we show that this simplified model does not reproduce the reported asymmetries in the velocity profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The root mean square errors are 16.8° and 7° for the elbow and shoulder flexion angles when comparing model predictions with experimental data.
source: The root mean square errors are 16.8° and 7° for the elbow and shoulder flexion angles.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a quantitative comparison between model and experimental data.

claim: After determining the movement duration for different widths, parameters a and b in Fitts' law were obtained as 0.0234 and 0.0550, respectively.
source: After determining the MD for different widths, we perform a least-squares fit to determine parameters a and b in Fitts' law, obtaining values of 0.0234 and 0.0550, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a result of least-squares fitting.

claim: The parameters a and b are within the range of values determined from experimental data in Goldberg et al., 2014.
source: These values are within the range of values a ∈ [0.0047, 0.5239] and b ∈ [0.0393,0.1987] determined from the experimental data in Goldberg et al., 2014, where subjects reach with a mouse to targets of various distances and widths on a computer screen.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with experimental data from Goldberg et al., 2014.

claim: There is good agreement between the model's predicted movement duration and Fitts' law (R2 = 0.974).
source: In Figure 3C, we show that there is good agreement between the model's predicted MD (averaged over 10 runs) and Fitts' law (R2 = 0.974).
evidence: The claim is supported by the R2 value calculated from model predictions.

claim: The movement duration becomes more variable when the target size decreases as the optimization becomes more likely to fall in local minima.
source: Note that the MD becomes more variable when the target size decreases as the optimization becomes more likely to fall in local minima.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the optimization process and observed data.

claim: The feature of increased movement duration variability with smaller targets is present in experimental data but not predicted by previous models.
source: This feature is also present in the experimental data (Figure 3A and B), although it is not predicted by previous models (Harris and Wolpert, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with experimental data and citation to Harris and Wolpert, 1998.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the model's mean predicted movement duration and the mean of the experimental data is 0.959 (p<0.001).
source: This was verified as the correlation coefficient between our model's mean predicted MD (as it varies with the index of difficulty) and the mean of the experimental data (Goldberg et al., 2014; Figure 3A) is 0.959 (p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a statistical result comparing model and experimental data.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the standard deviations of the model and the experimental data is 0.70 (p=0.0167).
source: The correlation coefficient between the standard deviations of our model and the experimental data is 0.70 (p=0.0167).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a statistical result.

claim: For the torque-driven model, there is good agreement between the model's predicted mean movement duration and Fitts' law (R2 = 0.88).
source: There is again good agreement between the model's predicted mean MD (averaged over 10 runs) and Fitts' law (R2 = 0.88).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a result for the torque-driven model shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correlations between the torque-driven model's predicted means and standard deviations and the experimental data are weak and not statistically significant.
source: However, the correlations between the predicted means and standard deviations and the experimental data in Goldberg et al., 2014 (Figure 3A) are weak (R2 = 0.17 and R2 = 0.39, respectively) and not statistically significant.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a statistical result for the torque-driven model.

claim: With a less effective trajectory optimizer, the model's predicted movement duration means are still in very close agreement with Fitts' law (R2 = 0.969).
source: In Figure 3—figure supplement 2, we see that model's predicted MD means are still in close agreement with Fitts' law (R2 = 0.969).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlation coefficients between the predicted means and standard deviations with experimental data are significant: 0.82 (p=0.007) and 0.83 (p=0.006).
source: The correlation coefficients between the predicted means and standard deviations with experimental data (Figure 3A) are significant: 0.82 (p=0.007) and 0.83 (p=0.006).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a statistical result.

claim: Fitts' law emerges even without the muscle activations term in the cost function.
source: We performed an additional experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) to show that Fitts' law emerges even without this term in the cost function.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Models with unrealistic active force–length relationships produced movement durations consistent with Fitts' law, but predictions were not correlated with experimental data.
source: We found that these models produced MDs that are consistent with Fitts' law, but the predictions were not correlated with the experimental data in Goldberg et al., 2014 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 1 and comparison with Goldberg et al., 2014.

claim: Reaches to smaller targets are slower than those to larger targets, as predicted by Fitts' law.
source: Behaviorally, we find that reaches to smaller targets are slower than those to larger targets, as predicted by Fitts' law (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The movement durations to smaller targets are more variable than to larger targets (standard deviation of 0.257 s compared to 0.234 s; p=0.0262).
source: The MDs to smaller targets are more variable than to larger targets (i.e., a standard deviation of 0.257 s compared to 0.234 s; p=0.0262).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with statistical support.

claim: Reaches to smaller targets exhibit less variability in the population-level motor cortical preparatory neural state than reaches to larger targets.
source: Neurally, we find that reaches to smaller targets exhibit less variability in the population-level motor cortical preparatory neural state than reaches to larger targets (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by neural data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The contribution of preparatory variability to movement variability is larger for smaller targets than larger targets.
source: Intersecting this with findings that nearly half of movement variability can be attributed to preparatory variability for a highly practiced task (Churchland et al., 2006a), we find that the contribution of preparatory variability to movement variability is larger for smaller targets than larger targets (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by neural data shown in Figure 4E and citation to Churchland et al., 2006a.

claim: Signal-dependent noise scales with the size of the control signal.
source: Signal-dependent noise or 'motor noise' has been shown across a variety of experiments, where noise scales in proportion to the size of the motor command being generated (e.g., Jones et al., 2002; Matthews, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2002 and Matthews, 1996.

claim: The speed-accuracy tradeoff, as described by Fitts' law, emerges even without the presence of motor noise.
source: This model revealed that the speed-accuracy tradeoff, as described by Fitts' law, emerges even without the presence of motor noise, which is commonly believed to underlie the speed-accuracy tradeoff.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a key finding of the study.

claim: The contribution of preparatory neural activity to movement duration variability is greater for smaller targets than larger targets.
source: We found that the contribution of preparatory neural activity to movement duration (MD) variability is greater for smaller targets than larger targets, and that movements to smaller targets exhibit less variability in population-level preparatory activity, but greater MD variability.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a key finding from neural analyses.

claim: Fitts' law emerges from greater task demands constraining the optimization landscape in a fashion that reduces the number of 'good' control solutions.
source: These results propose a new theory underlying the speed-accuracy tradeoff: Fitts' law emerges from greater task demands constraining the optimization landscape in a fashion that reduces the number of 'good' control solutions (i.e., faster reaches).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as the proposed new theory.

claim: The speed-accuracy tradeoff could be a consequence of motor planning variability and not exclusively signal-dependent noise.
source: Thus, contrary to current beliefs, the speed-accuracy tradeoff could be a consequence of motor planning variability and not exclusively signal-dependent noise.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: A widely held theory posits that signal-dependent noise is a sufficient theory to explain Fitts' law.
source: A widely held theory, initially proposed by Harris and Wolpert, posits that signal-dependent noise (i.e., 'motor noise' present at the neuromuscular junction) that scales with the size of the control signal is a sufficient theory to explain Fitts' law (Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Lunardini et al., 2015; McCrea and Eng, 2005; Peternel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Lunardini et al., 2015; McCrea and Eng, 2005; Peternel et al., 2017.

claim: Prior work has employed simple one-dimensional linear systems or torque-driven two-joint models of the arm to study the speed-accuracy tradeoff.
source: In support of this theory, a large body of prior work has employed simple one-dimensional linear systems or torque-driven two-joint models of the arm that are restricted to moving in a plane to study the speed-accuracy tradeoff (e.g., Flash and Hogan, 1985; Fagg et al., 2002; Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Alexander, 1997; DeWolf et al., 2016; Sketch et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The musculoskeletal model proposed by Saul and colleagues was previously used to track experimental kinematics, but not synthesize movements de novo.
source: The musculoskeletal model proposed by Saul and colleagues was previously used to track experimental kinematics, but not synthesize movements de novo.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as background information.

claim: The movements are synthesized by minimizing a cost function based on end-point accuracy and squared muscle activation terms.
source: The movements are synthesized by minimizing a cost function based on end-point accuracy and squared muscle activation terms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the method.

claim: The squared muscle activation term is used as an approximation to metabolic power consumption.
source: We use the squared muscle activation term as an approximation to metabolic power consumption (Millard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Millard et al., 2013.

claim: The asymmetry in the velocity profile with movement speed can be explained in terms of optimal control theory.
source: We show that the asymmetry in the velocity profile with movement speed can be explained in terms of optimal control theory, as opposed to it either representing some unexplained feature, or resulting from constraints in the neural architecture (Bullock and Grossberg, 1988), or a learned strategy when approaching a target (Beggs and Howarth, 1972), or time-varying cost constraints (Nagasaki, 1989), or signal-dependent noise with a minimum variance model (Tanaka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model results and citations to alternative theories.

claim: For more challenging tasks, the trajectory optimizer tends to find less effective solutions than other undiscovered but possible solutions.
source: Our theory suggests that for more challenging tasks (e.g., reaching to smaller targets), the trajectory optimizer tends to find less effective solutions (i.e., slower reaches) than other undiscovered but possible solutions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as part of the proposed theory.

claim: For less challenging tasks, the optimizer tends to find more effective solutions.
source: For less challenging tasks (e.g., reaching to larger targets), the optimizer tends to find more effective solutions (i.e., faster reaches).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as part of the proposed theory.

claim: With more challenging tasks, previously effective solutions are discarded as they do not produce trajectories that reach the target.
source: With more challenging tasks, previously effective solutions are discarded as they do not produce trajectories that reach the target; the smaller set of effective solutions makes it more likely for the optimizer to converge to a less effective solution.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as part of the proposed theory.

claim: Some features of human movement are attributable to planning variability rather than execution noise alone.
source: The crux of our theory is that some features of human movement are attributable to planning variability rather than execution noise (e.g., Figure 4 and Churchland et al., 2006a for related evidence).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 4 and citation to Churchland et al., 2006a.

claim: Nearly 60% of the movement duration variability is attributed to planning variability when reaching to the smaller target.
source: Our results show that nearly 60% of the MD variability is attributed to planning variability when reaching to the smaller target (and that the MD standard deviation is large relative to the mean with a coefficient of variation of 0.4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a result from the neural analyses.

claim: Motor planning variability can account for more than 75% of the movement duration difference when reaching to the large and small target.
source: This suggests that planning variability can account for more than 75% of the MD difference when reaching to the large and small target (i.e., 0.6 × 258/200).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the neural data.

claim: Bullock and Grossberg, 1988 proposed that the speed-dependent asymmetry in the velocity profile arises due to neural dynamics.
source: Bullock and Grossberg, 1988 proposed that the speed-dependent asymmetry in the velocity profile arises due to neural dynamics and that models based on optimal control always predict symmetric velocity profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bullock and Grossberg, 1988.

claim: Asymmetric velocity profiles in reaching movements arise from optimal control methods with realistic biomechanical models.
source: Our work demonstrates that asymmetric velocity profiles in reaching movements arise from optimal control methods with realistic biomechanical models, without relying on other modeling assumptions such as time-varying jerk constraints (Nagasaki, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model results and citation to Nagasaki, 1989.

claim: This feature did not emerge in earlier work using simplified biomechanical models.
source: This feature did not emerge in earlier work using simplified biomechanical models (Guigon et al., 2007; Harris and Wolpert, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guigon et al., 2007 and Harris and Wolpert, 1998.

claim: The elbow flexors undergoing an eccentric contraction have a larger force generating capacity at higher speeds due to the force–velocity relationship of muscle.
source: The elbow flexors undergoing an eccentric contraction have a larger force generating capacity at higher speeds due to the force–velocity relationship of muscle (Millard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Millard et al., 2013.

claim: The hypothesis that faster movements have a later peak velocity due to muscle force-velocity properties is supported by the fact that this property does not arise in a torque-driven model.
source: Our hypothesis is that this explains why faster movements have a later peak velocity. We have verified that this property does not arise in a torque-driven model (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which supports the hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison between muscle-based and torque-driven models.

claim: There is evidence of an improved signal-to-noise ratio during motor skill learning in rodents.
source: Indeed, there is evidence of an improved signal-to-noise ratio during motor skill learning in rodents (Kargo and Nitz, 2004), but their mechanism proposes a reduction in signal-independent noise and pre-burst firing rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kargo and Nitz, 2004.

claim: More stringent task constraints reduce the space of possible control solutions, thereby removing effective solutions from the search landscape.
source: Our analyses reveal that more stringent task constraints reduce the space of possible control solutions, thereby removing effective solutions from the search landscape (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analyses and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: For challenging tasks, the patterns of neural activity found during initial optimization correspond to ineffective solutions, leading to suboptimal behavior.
source: Thus, for challenging tasks, the patterns of neural activity found during initial optimization (i.e., learning) correspond to ineffective solutions, leading to suboptimal behavior, e.g., reaching slower to smaller targets, consistent with Fitts' law.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as part of the proposed theory.

claim: A testable prediction of the theory is that neural variability during motor planning should progressively decrease as the shift in performance occurs during practice.
source: A testable prediction of our theory is that the neural variability during motor planning should progressively decrease as the shift in performance occurs during practice (and as the central nervous system converges to better motor plans).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a testable prediction.

claim: The broader mechanism for motor control likely engages both the mechanism proposed here and certain aspects of signal-dependent noise.
source: While our theory does not account for signal-dependent noise, the broader mechanism for motor control likely engages both the mechanism proposed here and certain aspects of signal-dependent noise.
evidence: The claim is stated as a speculation about the broader mechanism.

claim: A realistic biomechanical model allows for more accurate estimation of the optimization landscape.
source: We posit that a realistic biomechanical model, as described here, allows for more accurate estimation of the optimization landscape (i.e., how the local optima are situated with respect to the control solutions).
evidence: The claim is stated as a hypothesis based on the results.

claim: The realistic biomechanical model produces results that are strongly correlated with prior experimental findings, while simplified models are not.
source: This explains why the realistic biomechanical model produces results that are strongly correlated with prior experimental findings (Goldberg et al., 2014), while all of our simplified models (which includes the torque-driven, fewer muscles, unrealistic force-length relationships, and unrealistic cost function models) are not statistically correlated with prior experimental findings since they are more likely to synthesize unrealistic movements (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model results with experimental data and shown in Table 1.

claim: Fitts' law emerges both with a standard and a less effective optimizer.
source: Our experiments show that Fitts' law emerges both with a standard and a less effective optimizer.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a result of the experiments.

claim: Imposing progressively more stringent accuracy constraints removes good solutions from the optimization landscape, resulting in performance degradation and thus yielding Fitts' law.
source: This follows from the fact that for an optimizer with a given performance (i.e., measured by the number of samples and trials that it can explore), imposing progressively more stringent accuracy constraints removes good solutions from the optimization landscape, resulting in performance degradation and thus yielding Fitts' law.
evidence: The claim is stated as an explanation based on the optimization results.

claim: A theory based purely on signal-dependent motor noise does not predict that more severe accuracy constraints cause more movement duration variability.
source: A theory based purely on signal-dependent motor noise does not predict that more severe accuracy constraints cause more MD variability, as seen in the experimental data.
evidence: The claim is stated as a contrast with the proposed theory and supported by experimental data.

claim: The difference between the fastest trials to the smallest and largest targets amounts to 0.04 s in the computational experiments.
source: The differences in durations between the fastest trials to the smallest and largest targets provide an indicator of the role of limb dynamics in the speed-accuracy tradeoff. The fastest trial approaches the limit of what is dynamically feasible given enough trials. In our computational experiments, this difference amounts to 0.04 s.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a result from the computational experiments.

claim: The average difference from the experimental data is 0.04 ± 0.03 s.
source: The average difference from the experimental data is also 0.04 ± 0.03 s (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: 65% of the total difference in movement duration is attributable to motor planning variability.
source: The difference between the mean durations to the two targets minus the difference between the fastest reaches (65% of the total difference in Figure 3C) is attributable to motor planning variability (as we have excluded the roles of limb dynamics and execution noise), which is the dominant factor behind the speed-accuracy tradeoff in our results.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the data in Figure 3C.

claim: A current theory suggests that movement period neural activity evolves from an initial condition set in premotor and primary motor cortex.
source: Turning our attention to neural mechanisms underlying motor cortical function, a current theory suggests that movement period neural activity evolves from an initial condition (termed the neural population preparatory state) set in premotor and primary motor cortex (Shenoy et al., 2013; Vyas et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shenoy et al., 2013 and Vyas et al., 2020a.

claim: Generating initial conditions closer to the optimal initial condition results in behavioral benefits.
source: Different movements have different initial conditions and generating initial conditions closer to the optimal initial condition results in behavioral benefits (Afshar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Afshar et al., 2011.

claim: Trial-by-trial behavior variability is strongly linked to neural variability during motor preparation, even for highly practiced movements.
source: Furthermore, trial-by-trial behavior variability is strongly linked to neural variability during motor preparation, even for highly practiced movements (Churchland et al., 2006a), and motor learning is strongly linked with systematic changes to neural activity during motor preparation, where neural activity during motor preparation plays a causal role in error-driven learning (Vyas et al., 2018; Vyas et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Churchland et al., 2006a, Vyas et al., 2018, and Vyas et al., 2020b.

claim: If movement planning variability is a dominant factor underlying the speed-accuracy tradeoff, then the proportion of movement duration variability explained by preparatory variability should increase with reaches to smaller targets.
source: If movement planning variability is a dominant factor underlying the speed-accuracy tradeoff, then the proportion of MD variability explained by preparatory variability should increase with reaches to smaller targets (otherwise motor planning does not contribute to the speed-accuracy tradeoff).
evidence: The claim is stated as a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: The hypothesis that the proportion of movement duration variability explained by preparatory variability increases with reaches to smaller targets has been experimentally verified.
source: We have experimentally verified this prediction (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: If the speed-accuracy tradeoff was solely caused by execution noise, then movement duration variability would be expected to decrease when planning variability decreases.
source: If the speed-accuracy tradeoff was solely caused by execution noise, then we would expect MD variability to decrease when planning variability decreases.
evidence: The claim is stated as a logical expectation under an alternative hypothesis.

claim: The results are consistent with the theory that some of the effective control solutions have to be discarded when reaching to smaller targets.
source: These results, however, are consistent with our theory (Figure 5), which suggests that some of the effective control solutions (i.e., motor plans for fast reaches) have to be discarded when reaching to smaller targets (i.e., variability in preparatory activity decreases, while MD variability increases).
evidence: The claim is supported by the results and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The movement variability resulting from motor planning variability can be modeled with the solutions found from stochastic optimization.
source: Our work presumes that the movement variability resulting from motor planning variability can be modeled with the solutions found from stochastic optimization (but we do not claim that a stochastic optimization is actually being literally performed by the brain during motor planning).
evidence: The claim is stated as an assumption of the modeling approach.

claim: At convergence, when reaching to smaller targets, the motor plans tend to be less effective because of task constraints.
source: Rather, our results show that, at convergence (i.e., the solutions from stochastic optimization), when reaching to smaller targets, the motor plans tend to be less effective (i.e., slower reaches) because of task constraints (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the optimization results and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The reaches to the large target that also do not reach the small target are on average faster than the reaches to the small target.
source: When comparing the reaches to a large and a small target, we have empirically verified that the reaches to the large target that also do not reach the small target are on average faster than the reaches to the small target.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an empirical verification.

claim: The computational model implements motor planning stochasticity with covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES).
source: Our computational model implements motor planning stochasticity with covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES), which operates by applying Gaussian noise on an initial motor plan.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the method.

claim: Motor planning stochasticity could arise as simply as noise on an initial motor plan due to variability in the inputs from other brain regions.
source: It is unknown how motor planning stochasticity arises at the individual neural and neural population level, but it could be as simple as noise on an initial motor plan (e.g., due to variability in the inputs from other brain regions [Vyas et al., 2020b]).
evidence: The claim is stated as speculation with citation to Vyas et al., 2020b.

claim: Trial-to-trial variability in the preparatory state in the model has been approximated via sampling from a Gaussian distribution.
source: We have approximated the trial-to-trial variability in the preparatory state in our model via sampling from a Gaussian distribution.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the modeling approach.

claim: When implementing planning variability in a computational model, movement durations are obtained that are consistent with Fitts' law and experimental findings on movement duration variability.
source: When implementing planning variability in a computational model, we obtain MDs that are consistent with Fitts' law and experimental findings on MD variability (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no causal evidence linking neural variability during preparation and Fitts' law.
source: First, we do not have causal evidence linking neural variability during preparation and Fitts' law (although we have a causal link between variability during preparation and Fitts' law in our computational model).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a caveat.

claim: The preparatory state encodes important parameters of the upcoming reach, such as distance, direction, and speed.
source: Finally, while the preparatory state does not encode the whole reach trajectory (as the model's motor plan does), it does encode important parameters of the upcoming reach, such as distance, direction, and speed (Messier and Kalaska, 2000; Churchland et al., 2006b; Even-Chen et al., 2019; Vyas et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Messier and Kalaska, 2000; Churchland et al., 2006b; Even-Chen et al., 2019; Vyas et al., 2020a.

claim: Fitts' law is tightly linked to movement planning and not just movement execution.
source: One tantalizing interpretation of our results is that Fitts' law is tightly linked to movement planning (which includes many of the aspects of the preparatory activity analyzed here) and not just movement execution.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The difficulty associated with finding optimal solutions for challenging tasks could be akin to finding the optimal preparatory neural states.
source: The difficulty associated with finding optimal solutions for challenging tasks could then be akin to finding the optimal preparatory neural states (as well as learning the appropriate movement period dynamics), where task constraints govern the optimization landscape, as suggested by our theory.
evidence: The claim is stated as a speculation based on the theory.

claim: The wrist and finger joints were locked in the model.
source: We have locked the wrist and finger joints.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the model.

claim: The optimization uses 500 iterations and a population size of 20 in CMA-ES.
source: We use 500 iterations and a population size of 20 in CMA-ES, which takes about 3 hr of computation time (after parallelization) with two Intel Xeon CPU E5-4640 processors.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the optimization parameters.

claim: The optimization is initialized with all the knots set to 0.1.
source: We initialize the optimization with all the knots set to 0.1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the initialization.

claim: Right-handed subjects gave written informed consent approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board.
source: Right-handed subjects (n = 4, age = 27 ± 3, mean ± std, two males, two females) gave written informed consent approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Subjects are instructed to reach the target pose at a comfortable speed, without moving their trunk or feet.
source: Subjects are instructed to reach the target pose at a comfortable speed, without moving their trunk or feet.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a description of the experimental procedure.
